title: Pay for the harm you do
hook: Two ad slots, three bidders. If the winner doesn't pay their own bid, what do they pay?

doesNotKnow: that charging each winner the value their presence costs everyone else makes honest bids best, even with several slots

misconception: In a multi-slot ad auction each winner should pay their own bid.
objective: The learner can explain that under VCG the top winner pays the value the others lose because of them (here $65 without X minus $30 with X, so $35), and that no bid leaves X better off than the honest one.

claims.text: Without X, Y and Z get $65 of value (Y takes the top slot, 10 x $6 = $60, Z the second, 5 x $1 = $5); with X on top, Y gets 5 x $6 = $30 and Z gets nothing; so X pays the $35 gap, not the $70 its own bid would charge. At the honest $7 the stage line read both sums: 'Without X: Y $60 + Z $5 = $65 · With X: Y $30 + Z $0 = $30'.
claims.source: Demo.tsx outcome(7) and sums(): othersWithout = 60 + 5 = 65, othersWith = 30, pay = 35; X's own bid x clicks = 7 x 10 = 70. claims.text: By the same rule, with honest bids Y pays $5 and Z pays $0.
claims.source: Y: others' value without Y = 7 x 10 + 1 x 5 = 75, with Y = 70, so 5. Z: without Z = 70 + 30 = 100, with Z = 100, so 0. Re-run in node (ncm-e00). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own VCG script: Y pays 75 - 70 = 5, Z pays 100 - 100 = 0 (Z unplaced).

claims.text: With Y bidding $6 and Z $1, no bid from $0 to $10 gives X more than the honest $7: bids of $6 to $10 tie at $35 kept, bids of $1 to $5 put X in the second slot keeping $30; X's bid only picks the slot, the others' bids set the price.
claims.source: X's profit by bid 0..10 = [0,30,30,30,30,30,35,35,35,35,35] (ties go to X; a $0 bid takes no slot). Demo.tsx outcome(b); matches the brief's re-run. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own script, X's kept value for bids 0..10 with ties to X = 0,30,30,30,30,30,35,35,35,35,35; reveal prints outcome(7).keep and outcome(3).keep.

claims.text: This payment rule is the VCG mechanism, under which bidding your true value is a dominant strategy.
claims.source: Vickrey 1961 (J. Finance 16), Clarke 1971 (Public Choice 11), Groves 1973 (Econometrica 41); Easley and Kleinberg 2010, ch. 15. Fact-checker to confirm attribution. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Attribution from own knowledge (sources not opened, network blocked): Vickrey 1961 J. Finance 16 'Counterspeculation, auctions, and competitive sealed tenders'; Clarke 1971 Public Choice 11 'Multipart pricing of public goods'; Groves 1973 Econometrica 41 'Incentives in teams'. Truthful bidding is a dominant strategy under VCG (standard; also stated as the VCG benchmark in the EOS 2007 abstract snippet). E&K ch. 15 'Sponsored Search Markets' covers VCG (placement from own knowledge, confident).

claims.text: The lesson is a simplified model: fixed clicks per slot, invented values, Y and Z bid their values, ties go to X.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: Y bids $6, Z bids $1; ties go to X' and the reveal's last line. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Matches the reveal's muted line and stage chip; outcome() implements fixed clicks, invented values, ties to X.

recall.question: Under the pay-the-harm rule, the others would get $50 of value without you and $20 with you in the top slot. What do you pay?
recall.why: You pay the value your presence costs everyone else: $50 without you minus $20 with you, $30.
